endings.user: The train. I don't mind the walk.

endings.user: The bus. I can read the whole way without changing.
endings.moshi: That's a great reason. Fifty minutes of reading adds up to a lot of books.

turns.speaker: user

endings.user: Yeah, I go out most weekends.

turns.text: Okay, you have options. There's an airport bus in twenty minutes, or a taxi would get you there faster but cost a lot more. What do you want to do?

endings.user: The bus. I've got enough time.
endings.moshi: Good. It leaves from the stop outside the main entrance, so head there now.

endings.user: Taxi. I'm not risking it.
endings.moshi: Understood. The taxi rank is just outside the station, and it should take about thirty minutes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The concert just ended and there are four of us heading the same way home.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Nice. The night bus leaves in twenty minutes and takes about an hour. Split four ways, a taxi wouldn't cost much each. Which way?

contexts.pending: night bus or shared taxi after concert
think_reask: So, getting home from the concert. Night bus, or split a taxi?
Right, the four of you. Bus or cab?
welcome_back: Still need to get you all home. The night bus, or a shared taxi?
So, cheap and slow, or quick and split four ways?

endings.user: Taxi. My feet are done.
endings.moshi: Fair. Agree who pays up front and settle up after, it saves an awkward moment at the door.

endings.user: Night bus. Someone in our group is broke this month.
endings.moshi: Kind choice. Sit near the driver and the hour will fly by with four of you chatting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got my toddler and a big pushchair today.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The nearest station only has stairs. The next one has a lift but it's ten minutes further.

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: So, risk waking him on the stairs, or take the longer walk?

contexts.pending: nearer station with stairs or further one with lift
think_reask: So, with the pushchair, stairs nearby or the lift further on?
Which station are you heading for?
Stairs and carrying, or the walk to the lift?
welcome_back: The pushchair problem is still waiting. Close station with stairs, or the one with the lift?
So, which station, now that you've had a minute?

endings.user: The lift. Let him sleep.
endings.moshi: Good choice. The walk might even keep him dozing, the motion usually helps.

endings.user: The stairs. Someone always offers to help.
endings.moshi: Often true. Fold anything loose into the basket first so it's easier to lift with a stranger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've missed the last connecting train. I'm stuck at a junction station and it's almost midnight.

turns.speaker: moshi

welcome_back: Your overnight plan was still undecided. Station or hotel?
So, about tonight. Hotel down the road, or the waiting room?
The first train is still at quarter to six. Where are you spending the night?

endings.user: The hotel. I need a proper bed.
endings.moshi: Sensible. Set two alarms, and ask the desk if they serve early coffee.

endings.user: I'll wait here. It's only six hours.
endings.moshi: Okay. Find out if the waiting room stays open all night, and keep your bag on your lap.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm choosing between two flats for next term. One's right on the tram line but pricier.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And the cheaper one?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Bus plus a transfer, about forty minutes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: So extra rent versus time every day. Which matters more right now?

contexts.pending: pricier flat on tram line or cheaper with bus transfer

Which flat are you going for?
welcome_back: Your flat decision was still hanging. Rent, or commute time?
So, which wins, the tram flat or the cheaper one?
We'd got to rent versus time. Where's your head at?

endings.user: The cheaper one. I'll study on the bus.
endings.moshi: Plenty of people do. Forty minutes is enough to get through a chapter each way.

endings.user: The tram one. I'd rather sleep in.
endings.moshi: Honestly, that extra time adds up. Over a year, it's days of your life back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Tomorrow's the rail strike and I've got a job interview across the city at ten.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stressful timing. There's a replacement bus service, or you could take a bike from the share scheme. Which do you trust more?

welcome_back: Getting to the interview was still the open bit. Bus, or bike?
So, for tomorrow morning, which plan?

endings.user: The bike. I can't trust the buses on a strike day.
endings.moshi: Good. Leave early, take it gently so you don't arrive sweaty, and bring a spare shirt in your bag.

endings.user: The bus. I'll get the first one.
endings.moshi: Smart. Replacement buses fill up fast, so the earliest one gives you a safety margin.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I use a wheelchair, and I'm off to the stadium on Saturday.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Got it. The direct bus is low floor all the way. The metro is faster, but the lift at the stadium station has been out a lot. Which are you leaning towards?

contexts.pending: low floor bus or faster metro with unreliable lift
think_reask: So, for Saturday, the reliable bus or the quicker metro?
Bus or metro to the stadium?
welcome_back: The stadium trip still needs a route. Bus, or metro?
So, are you risking the metro lift, or sticking with the bus?

endings.user: The bus. I don't want to get stuck underground.
endings.moshi: Totally fair. The low floor buses have a ramp, so just signal the driver as it pulls in.

endings.user: Metro, but I'll check the lift status first.
endings.moshi: Good idea. Most networks post lift outages online, so look on the morning of the match.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I spend two hours a day on the train and I can never get any work done.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lot of lost time. You could pay for the quiet carriage upgrade, or keep standard and try noise cancelling headphones. Which sounds better?

welcome_back: The work on the train question is still open. Quiet carriage, or headphones?

endings.user: Headphones. A one time cost.
endings.moshi: Makes sense. Pair them with a seat away from the doors and you'll get a lot more done.

endings.user: The upgrade. I need the table and the plug.
endings.moshi: That's a good point, the power socket alone is worth it on a two hour day.

endings.user: One change. More changes would confuse her.
endings.moshi: Then send her a photo of the platform signs so she knows what to look for.

endings.user: Two changes. Her knees can't do long walks.
endings.moshi: Good thinking. Tell her she has plenty of time at each stop, so she doesn't rush.

So, the hospital. Entrance bus or the quicker one?
welcome_back: The two buses were nearly at the stop. Which one did you go for?
So, door to door, or faster and a short walk?

endings.user: The fast one. I can walk a few streets.
endings.moshi: Good. Get off at the stop by the park, then it's straight ahead past the pharmacy.

endings.user: The slow one. I've got a bad ankle.
endings.moshi: Then that's the right call. It's a slower ride, but no walking at the other end.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm visiting a big city next week and I've never used a subway before. Any tips?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Download the city's transit app before you go. It shows routes, live times and which exit to use.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know / which direction to go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Platforms are usually labeled by the last station on the line. Find your stop on the map, then follow signs for the end station in that direction.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That makes sense. What about rush hour?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try to avoid roughly seven to nine in the morning and five to seven in the evening. If you can't, stand to the side and let people off first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, thanks. I feel less nervous now.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'll do great. Most people figure it out after one or two rides.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I get really motion sick on buses. Is there anything that helps?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sit near the front, facing forward, and look out the window at the horizon. Reading or scrolling usually makes it worse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always read / on my commute, though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Audiobooks or podcasts are a great swap. You keep the story without staring at a page.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hmm, I never thought of that. Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fresh air helps, so open a window if you can. Some people also find ginger candies settle their stomach.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll try the podcast thing first.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. Let me know if you want some podcast suggestions.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I bring my bike on the train?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: On most regional trains, yes, but often not during rush hour. Look for the carriages with a bike symbol on the door.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need a ticket for it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many operators charge a small bike fee or need a reservation on long distance trains. Check your operator's website before you go.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Actually, I'm also thinking / about getting a folding bike instead.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great option for commuting. Folded bikes usually count as luggage, so you can bring them anytime for free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Aren't they slow, though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A bit slower than a regular bike, but for short rides to and from the station you'll hardly notice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandson says I should use the bus instead of driving into town. I'm seventy-two and I haven't taken a bus in years.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of people rediscover the bus later in life. Many cities offer a free or discounted senior pass, too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How would I / find out about that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Your local transit office or the town hall can tell you. You usually just need a photo ID showing your age.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And where do I get on? I don't want to look silly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wave to the driver as the bus comes, then get on at the front and show your pass. Drivers are used to questions, so feel free to ask which stop is yours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That doesn't sound so bad.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It really isn't. And no parking to worry about in town.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What are the actual rules in a quiet carriage? My neighbour keeps taking calls.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Generally, no phone calls, no music without headphones, and keep conversations to a whisper.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I say something to him?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A polite word is fine. Something like, this is the quiet carriage, would you mind taking that in the corridor.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if he / just ignores me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then let the train staff know. It's their job to enforce it, and you don't have to get into an argument.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I hate confrontation.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most people are just distracted and apologise straight away. You might be surprised.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My train was over an hour late yesterday. Can I get money back?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very likely. Most operators pay compensation for delays, and an hour usually gets you a good chunk of the fare.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I claim?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Go to the operator's website and look for delay repay or something similar. You'll need your ticket details and the train time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I bought it / at the station though, a paper one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's fine. Take a photo of the ticket before you throw it away, and upload it with the claim.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there a deadline?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually around a month, so do it this week while you remember.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Brilliant, I didn't know this existed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I left my umbrella on the bus this morning. It was my grandad's. Any chance of getting it back?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Quite a good chance, actually. Lost items usually go to the depot first and then to a lost property office.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I find them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Call the bus company or fill in their lost property form. Tell them the route number, rough time, and describe the umbrella.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's black with a / wooden duck head handle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's distinctive, which helps a lot. Mention the duck handle, it'll stand out among all the plain black ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long do they keep stuff?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often a few weeks, so it's worth calling today.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I take a cello on the train? It's in a hard case.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually yes. Most trains allow musical instruments as long as they fit in the luggage space or you can hold them without blocking the aisle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A cello is quite big.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: True. On a busy commuter train it could be tough. On long distance trains, some people book a seat for the instrument.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A seat? For the cello?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It sounds funny, but it's common for musicians. The cello rides safely next to you instead of getting bumped in the rack.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually adorable.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just travel outside rush hour if you can.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I work late and take the last bus home. Sometimes it feels a bit sketchy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's understandable. Sitting near the driver is one of the simplest things you can do, there's always someone watching that area.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if someone / starts bothering me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Move seats, tell the driver, or get off at a busy stop. Most buses have a way to alert the driver quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I also have a long walk from the stop.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Share your location with a friend or housemate, and keep your keys ready before you get off. Some services also let you request a stop closer to your home at night.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Really? I'll ask about that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My son's eleven and wants to take the bus to school on his own. I'm terrified.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally normal feeling. Lots of parents do a few trial runs together first, then let him lead while you follow.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should he know?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Which stop to get off at, what to do if he misses it, and who to ask for help, like the driver.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He has a phone, but / it's always on low battery.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a small power bank in his bag is worth it. Also agree on a quick text when he arrives.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just one text?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: One text, so it feels like independence and not surveillance. He'll be prouder than you expect.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Long distance train tickets are so expensive. Any tricks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Booking ahead is the biggest one. Cheaper tickets usually go on sale about two or three months out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I never know my plans that far ahead.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then look into railcards if your country has them. They often cut a third off for a small yearly fee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there one for me? I'm / thirty one, so no student stuff.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There are often cards for people under thirty, for couples, for families, or for anyone travelling regularly. Check what's offered where you live.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Travelling off peak helps a lot. And splitting a journey into two tickets is sometimes cheaper than one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't get the fare zones on this metro map at all.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're usually rings around the centre. The more rings you cross, the more you pay.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So if I live in zone three and work in zone one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'd need a ticket covering zones one to three, even if you never stop in zone two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Even though I / just pass through it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, annoyingly. The fare is based on the whole area your journey covers, not just the ends.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I get off in zone four by accident?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you'd technically need to pay the difference. Most ticket machines can sort that out on the way out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got an hour on the train each way. I want to stop just scrolling and actually learn something.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great use of the time. A language app works well in short bursts, and you can do listening exercises with headphones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've tried apps. I get bored after a week.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then maybe pick something with a story. A course built around a podcast, or reading a novel in the language with a translation beside it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do like / mystery novels.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Easy mysteries written for learners exist in lots of languages. Each chapter fits nicely into a ride.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And on the way home when I'm tired?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Make the evening ride lighter, just listening. Mornings for effort, evenings for review.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is a park and ride worth it? I drive in every day and parking costs a fortune.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often, yes. You park on the edge of town for a flat fee and a bus takes you into the centre, usually with its own lanes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Doesn't the bus make it slower?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes it's actually quicker at rush hour, since buses skip the queues. And you don't circle around looking for a space.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much / would I save, roughly?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on your city, but many people save more than half compared to central parking. Check the weekly ticket, it's often cheaper still.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll give it a go next week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I get really panicky on packed trains. Like, heart racing, need to get off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That sounds really hard. A few things can help. Standing near the doors gives a sense of space and an easy way out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do try to stand there.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good. Slow breathing helps too, in for four counts and out for six. A longer out breath calms the body.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I / just travel at a different time?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If your work allows it, even half an hour earlier or later can make a huge difference to the crowds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My boss is pretty flexible.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then that's worth asking about. And if the panic keeps getting in the way, talking to a doctor is a good idea too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm taking the airport train with two massive suitcases. Any tips?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Board at the first carriage or the last one. They're usually quieter and closer to the luggage space.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if the racks are full?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep the cases beside you with the brakes on, out of the aisle. Most people understand on an airport line.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need / to worry about the gap?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lift the cases rather than rolling them over it. And let people off before you try to get on, it's much easier with space.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thanks, this is my first big trip alone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'll be fine. Have a wonderful time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I use a wheelchair and I'm nervous about the train trip next week. How does it work with ramps?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most rail companies let you book assistance in advance. Staff meet you at the platform with a ramp and help you on and off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How far in advance?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often a day or two ahead is enough, though booking earlier is safer. You can usually do it by phone or online.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if the / staff don't show up at my stop?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask the guard on the train to radio ahead. They can also deploy the ramp themselves on many trains.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's reassuring.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep your booking reference handy, it makes everything go faster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have six minutes to change trains tomorrow. Is that crazy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tight, but often fine if both trains are at the same station and on time. Is it one ticket for the whole trip?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, one booking.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then if you miss the connection because of a delay, you're usually allowed on the next train without paying again.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh good. How can I make the change faster?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look up the platform numbers in advance, and sit near the doors in the carriage closest to the exit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if it's / like a huge station?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then study the station map tonight. Knowing which way to turn saves more time than running.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Winter is coming and my commute always falls apart when it snows.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a common story. Checking live updates before you leave is the easiest habit to start.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I usually just go to the stop and hope.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try setting up alerts in your transit app for your route. You'll know about cancellations before you're standing in the cold.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And when it's / properly snowing, what then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Have a backup plan ready, maybe a different line or working from home. Decide it the night before so the morning isn't chaos.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good point. Anything for the actual waiting?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Layers, warm socks, and gloves you can use your phone in. A flask of tea doesn't hurt either.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've just landed, it's two in the morning, and I'm completely fried. Is there any public transport running?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many big cities have night buses or a night tram. Does your airport have a transit desk or a board near arrivals?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a board. It says night line N four.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's probably your night bus. Check where it ends up and whether it stops near where you're staying.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It goes / to the central station.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then from there you could walk or grab a short taxi. Night services usually run every half hour or so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I just want my bed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Almost there. Keep your bag close and stay awake on the ride.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is taking the bus actually better for the environment than driving? Be honest.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Generally yes, especially when the bus is reasonably full. Per passenger, a busy bus produces far less pollution than everyone driving.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And an empty bus at midnight?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's less impressive, fair. But the bus runs anyway, so you riding it adds almost nothing extra.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh. I never looked / at it that way.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a nice way to think about it. And trains, especially electric ones, are usually even better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I can feel smug on the train.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little smugness is allowed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yo, I'm sixteen. Is there some kind of student discount for the bus?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually, yes. Many cities have a youth or student card that gives cheaper fares, sometimes even half price.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I get one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Normally you apply online or at a ticket office with a photo and proof of age, like a passport or school ID.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do my parents / have to sign anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes, if you're under a certain age. Check the form, it'll say.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it work on weekends?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most do, so you can use it for going out with mates too, not just school.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sick, thanks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've just retired and I'd love to see the country by train. Where would you even start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: What a lovely plan. Scenic routes through mountains or along the coast are a good place to begin.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm not in a hurry at all.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then slow regional lines are your friend. They stop in small towns, and you can break the journey wherever you like.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My wife likes / comfort, though. She won't rough it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then mix it up. Take the slow scenic line by day, and book a nice hotel each evening. Some countries even have rail passes for older travellers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A pass sounds useful.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be great value if you're taking lots of trains in a few weeks. Shall I explain how they usually work?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yes please, another time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Of course. Enjoy planning it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I got fined on the tram because my ticket app crashed. I had actually paid! It's infuriating.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's maddening. You can usually appeal. Did the app show the purchase anywhere, like in your email or bank statement?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My bank shows the payment.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good, that's your evidence. Screenshot the payment with the date and time and send it along with your appeal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Where do I / even send it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The fine notice should list an address or website for appeals. Do it soon, there's often a short deadline.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They'll probably ignore me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Proof of payment usually wins these cases. Keep it calm and factual.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can we talk about people eating hot food on the bus? Someone had a curry this morning.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, a classic commuter complaint. Strong smelling food in an enclosed space is definitely a common annoyance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it even allowed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on the city. Some networks ban eating altogether, others just ask people to be considerate.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I just suffer.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pretty much, unless there's a clear rule. You could move seats or open a window if there is one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I did move. Three times.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's commitment. Maybe a little bottle of peppermint oil for emergencies?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The bus just drove straight past me. I was standing right at the stop!

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: So annoying. At some stops, the driver only stops if someone signals. Did you hold your arm out?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No. I didn't know I had to.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's worth doing every time, especially at quieter stops. A clear wave as the bus approaches is enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And getting off? I sometimes / miss my stop because I'm not sure when to press.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Press the stop button just after the bus leaves the stop before yours. You'll usually see a sign light up saying the bus is stopping.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I feel like I've been doing buses wrong for years.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You've just been lucky with busy stops. Now you're a pro.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm starting a job on an island and I'll commute by ferry. I get seasick in a bathtub.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ferries can be gentler than you'd think, especially bigger ones. Where you sit makes a huge difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Where's best?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Low down and in the middle of the boat, where it moves least. Looking out at the horizon helps your brain make sense of the motion.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about / pills or something?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Travel sickness tablets help many people, but some make you drowsy. A pharmacist can suggest one that's fine for work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And on rough days?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fresh air on deck can be better than sitting inside. And eat something light before, an empty stomach often makes it worse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: This is either going to be lovely or a disaster.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most regular passengers get used to it after a few weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm moving to a big city and I'm not taking my car. How do I plan my life around transit?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with where you'll live. Pick somewhere within a short walk of a frequent line, ideally one that runs late.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What counts as frequent?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Every ten minutes or better. Then you never really need a timetable, you just turn up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And groceries? I'm worried / about carrying everything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A small shop near home for daily things, and online delivery for the heavy stuff. A folding trolley also helps a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about weekends away?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rent a car or use car share for the odd trip. It's usually still cheaper than owning one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I bring my baby's pram onto the bus folded or does it have to be folded?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, I think you mean unfolded? On many buses, yes, there's a space for prams and wheelchairs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yes, sorry, unfolded. Long day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No worries. Wheelchair users usually get priority for that space, so you might be asked to move or fold it if someone needs it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fair enough. What if / it's already taken by another pram?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you might have to wait for the next bus or fold it. Some drivers allow two if there's room.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it, thanks.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Hope the rest of your day is gentler.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The timetable says every twelve minutes, but there's no actual time listed. How am I supposed to plan?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That means it's a frequent service. Instead of exact times, buses run at a regular rhythm, so you'll never wait longer than about twelve minutes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I just show up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Basically, yes. If you need to be somewhere for a fixed time, assume the worst wait and add it on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, and late / at night, does it change?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often. The frequency drops in the evenings, and then the timetable might switch to exact times. Check the bottom of the sign.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ah, there's a little section there.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the one. Those evening times are worth a photo.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm doing a ten hour overnight coach next week. I need survival tips.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Respect. A neck pillow, an eye mask and earplugs are the holy trinity.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Where should I sit?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Somewhere in the middle, away from the toilet and not right over the wheels. A window seat lets you lean and control the curtain.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about / food and stuff?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bring snacks and water, but nothing too salty. And wear layers, coaches swing from boiling to freezing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything to help actually sleep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Download a long, boring podcast. And put your shoes somewhere you'll find them in the dark.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Very specific advice.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Learned the hard way, I imagine, by many people.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We just adopted a dog and I don't drive. Can she come on the train with me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In lots of places, yes. Small dogs often travel free, and bigger ones might need a ticket or have to stay on a lead.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She's medium sized. A bit nervous.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then start with short, quiet trips outside rush hour. Bring treats and a blanket that smells like home.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does she need / a muzzle or anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some networks require one, others don't. Check your local rules, and practise with it at home first if needed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I didn't think about practising.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It really helps. A calm first trip makes the next ones much easier for both of you.

option_sets.lead_in: I just started a new job across town and I'm choosing how to get there.
options: The first option is the express bus, about thirty five minutes, but it's often packed.
Then there's the train, which is faster, but I'd have to walk fifteen minutes to the station.
Option three is a tram that's slower but stops right outside my building.
And the last one is biking to the train station and taking the train from there.
moshi_comment: Biking to the station and taking the train is probably the fastest and adds some exercise. The tram is the most relaxed choice since it's door to door. The express bus is fine, but crowding every day can wear you down.
Do you mind a bit of walking or biking in the morning? If not, the train is a great choice. If you want zero hassle, the tram's convenience is hard to beat.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm trying to figure out which transit pass to buy for the month.
options: One option is a monthly unlimited pass, which pays off if I ride more than about twice a day.
Another is a pay as you go card, which is cheaper if I only ride a few times a week.
Or there's a weekly pass, which I could buy only for the weeks I'm busy.
moshi_comment: If you commute every workday, the monthly pass almost always wins. Pay as you go is the cheapest if you mostly work from home. The weekly pass is a good middle option if your schedule changes a lot.
How many days a week do you usually ride? If it's four or five, get the monthly pass. If it's only one or two, pay as you go is the way to go.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm going from the city to the coast for a long weekend and I can't settle on how.
options: A direct coach leaves at seven in the morning, it's cheap but takes nearly five hours.
There's the fast train, about two and a half hours, but tickets are three times the price.
A slower regional train is in between on price and goes along the river, which is supposed to be beautiful.
moshi_comment: The fast train buys you the most beach time if money isn't tight. The coach is the budget winner, though five hours is a long sit. The regional train turns the trip itself into part of the holiday.
If it's a relaxing weekend, I'd pick the river train, it's reasonably priced and you get the views. Book the fast train only if you're arriving late Friday and every hour counts.

option_sets.lead_in: My daughter starts secondary school in September and we're working out how she'll get there.
options: The school bus picks up at the end of our road, but it leaves really early, at ten past seven.
She could take the public bus with her friends, it's later but involves one change in town.
Or I drop her at the train station on my way to work, and she takes one stop.
moshi_comment: The school bus is the simplest and safest, even if the early start hurts. The public bus with friends builds independence, but the change adds a chance to miss a connection. The train is quick, though it ties her to your work schedule.
For the first term, the school bus takes the pressure off everyone. Once she's settled and confident, the public bus with her friends is a nice step towards independence.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got a pile of luggage and I need to get from the airport into the old town.
options: The airport express train is quick, but from the central station it's a twenty minute walk over cobbles.
A shuttle bus goes right to the old town square, though it only runs every forty minutes.
Taxis are waiting outside, but the driver who brought my friend charged a ridiculous amount.
There's also a tram, cheap and frequent, but the carriages are small and usually crowded.
moshi_comment: With lots of luggage, the shuttle bus is probably your best bet, as it drops you right in the square. The express train is fast, but dragging bags over cobbles is miserable. The tram is cheap but crowded carriages and big bags don't mix.
Check when the next shuttle leaves. If it's soon, take it. If it's a long wait, a taxi from the official rank is worth it, just agree the price before you set off.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm finally ditching my car for commuting, and I need to pick a new routine.
options: I could cycle to the park and ride, then take the express bus the rest of the way.
Another way is the train from my village, which only runs twice an hour.
Or I join my neighbour's car share to the tram terminus and ride the tram in.
moshi_comment: The train is the cleanest swap, but twice an hour gives you little room if you miss one. Cycling to the park and ride adds exercise and the express bus is usually reliable. The car share is sociable, but you depend on your neighbour's timing.
If you want the most flexibility, cycling plus the express bus means you're never waiting on anyone. The train works too if you're the kind of person who's always early.
